questions.q: What kind of question does Qiskit's transpilation/depth-analysis tooling actually answer?
options: How many physical qubits an algorithm would need on future fault-tolerant hardware
How expensive a circuit is to run on today's or near-term noisy hardware -- circuit depth, gate counts, connectivity-driven routing overhead for a specific real backend
Whether an algorithm is theoretically correct
How much a cloud job will cost in dollars
questions.explain: Qiskit's transpiler rewrites circuits for a target's native gate set/connectivity and produces depth/gate-count numbers aimed at near-term, real-hardware feasibility questions.

questions.q: What kind of question does the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator answer, as contrasted with Qiskit's tooling?
options: The same question as Qiskit's transpiler, just with a different user interface

How many physical qubits and how much runtime an algorithm would need on FUTURE fault-tolerant hardware, under configurable qubit-technology and error-correction assumptions -- not how it runs on today's real devices
How to visually draw a quantum circuit
How to convert a Q# program into a Qiskit circuit
questions.explain: The Resource Estimator targets a different hardware era entirely -- projecting needs for fault-tolerant hardware that doesn't exist yet, not analyzing fit on today's noisy real devices.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say these two approaches are 'not competing solutions to the same problem'?
options: Because one of them doesn't actually work

Because they answer genuinely different questions aimed at different hardware eras -- today's real noisy hardware feasibility vs. future fault-tolerant hardware cost projection -- so neither is a substitute for the other
Because Qiskit and Azure Quantum cannot both be installed on the same machine
Because only one of them can be used with Python
questions.explain: The lesson's central distinction: Qiskit's tools are for near-term hardware feasibility, the Resource Estimator is for fault-tolerant-era planning -- different questions, not rival answers to one question.

questions.q: In the verified illustrative teleportation gate/step count comparison, what was the result, and what does it imply?
options: Q# needed twice as many steps as Qiskit, proving Q# is less efficient

Both counted to exactly 8 steps for the identical protocol, demonstrating that gate counts for the SAME algorithm don't change based on which language implements it -- the real tooling difference is about standardized future-hardware cost projection, not raw gate counting
Qiskit could not express the teleportation protocol at all
The step counts could not be compared because the languages are too different
questions.explain: Both implementations counted to exactly 8 steps, since the algorithm's actual quantum structure is identical regardless of syntax -- gate counting alone doesn't capture the real distinction between the two tools' resource-estimation approaches.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should Qiskit's research-paper-level work on fault-tolerant resource estimation be characterized relative to Azure Quantum's Resource Estimator?
options: As functionally identical, standardized, push-button services

As separate research tooling and papers from IBM/the community, not a single standardized, integrated, free, push-button service built into Qiskit's core toolchain the way the Resource Estimator is built into Azure Quantum
As nonexistent -- no such research exists
As strictly more accurate than Azure Quantum's Resource Estimator in every case
questions.explain: The lesson is careful to note that fault-tolerant resource-estimation research exists around Qiskit too, but it isn't integrated into the core toolchain as one standardized service the way Azure Quantum's Resource Estimator is -- an honest, specific distinction rather than an overstatement.
